Otolaryngology · published research

Hearing loss

In people, one small pre-exposure crossover trial found no protective benefit against temporary noise exposure and a wavelength-comparison trial found no significant hearing-test effect. A mouse noise-trauma study reported less threshold shift after peri-traumatic 808-nm treatment, but this is preclinical.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In people, one small pre-exposure crossover trial found no protective benefit against temporary noise exposure and a wavelength-comparison trial found no significant hearing-test effect. A mouse noise-trauma study reported less threshold shift after peri-traumatic 808-nm treatment, but this is preclinical.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Hearing > Hearing loss category contains 15 records: ten animal studies, two human randomized trials, one systematic review, one narrative review, and one commentary. Animal work includes eight rat and two mouse records, chiefly noise or ototoxicity models. The evidence addresses both prevention and treatment and should not be combined as if those were the same clinical question.

Human and clinical evidence

Williams et al. studied 30 adults in a crossover trial of near-infrared pre-exposure treatment before temporary noise exposure. The trial did not demonstrate protection against the measured temporary threshold shift (2024). Goodman et al. randomized 33 participants in a double-blind wavelength comparison and found no statistically or clinically significant effect on hearing tests (2013). These small studies do not establish benefit for prevention or recovery of established hearing loss. A vestibular-function publication in the database is not direct evidence of hearing restoration.

Animal evidence

Most of the ten animal records use noise or ototoxic injury. A mouse peri-traumatic study reported less hearing loss after 808-nm treatment given before and after noise exposure (Meuser et al. 2025). Other rat studies report selected improvements, but the models, timing, and endpoints vary. Animal findings cannot establish a preventive or therapeutic effect in people.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo clinical evidence was identified in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human studies use different wavelengths and schedules, while the mouse experiment applied 808 nm around the noise insult. Across the animal records, light source, exposure timing, dose, and auditory outcomes vary. A prophylactic protocol delivered before a controlled noise exposure cannot be assumed to treat chronic sensorineural hearing loss. Human protocols need clinically relevant exposure conditions, standardized audiometry, speech-in-noise testing, and adequate adverse-event monitoring.

Interpretation

Current human evidence is very limited and does not show reliable protection or treatment benefit. A positive mouse result merits replication with PBM-alone controls, but it does not change the clinical conclusion.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for prevention of temporary noise-related hearing loss in people Very low for treatment of established human hearing loss
Publications and records15 records in Hearing > Hearing loss.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains two small human randomized trials and ten animal studies, mainly noise or ototoxicity models. Neither human trial establishes a clinically meaningful hearing benefit. Animal findings are mixed and do not establish prevention or recovery in patients. Independent trials should prespecify hearing thresholds and speech outcomes, distinguish pre-exposure prevention from treatment, and include adequate follow-up.
